sections.title: Variables, Types & Coercion
sections.description: Understand let/const/var, primitive vs reference values, strict equality, and truthiness rules.

lessons.title: var, let, const & Temporal Dead Zone
lessons.summary: let and const are block-scoped and sit in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until their declaration executes, preventing accidental pre-initialization reads.
explanation: let and const are block-scoped and sit in the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ) until their declaration executes, preventing accidental pre-initialization reads.

Unlike var—which is function-scoped and hoisted with value undefined—accessing a let or const binding before its declaration throws a ReferenceError. Note that const prevents reassigning the binding, not mutating object properties.
Default to const for every binding; reach for let only when reassignment is genuinely required, and avoid var in modern code.

codeExample.title: Block Scope & TDZ Behavior

keyPoints: let and const are hoisted to block scope but uninitialized in the TDZ until evaluated.
const freezes the variable reference, NOT internal properties of objects or arrays.
for (let i = ...) creates a fresh lexical binding per iteration, solving classic closure bugs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using var in a loop with async callbacks and seeing the final value repeated
commonMistakes.fix: Use let in loop headers so each iteration captures its own binding.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming const makes an array or object deeply immutable
commonMistakes.fix: Use Object.freeze() (or structured copies) when you actually need runtime immutability.

interviewQA.question: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
interviewQA.answer: The period between entering a block scope and executing a let/const declaration during which referencing the variable throws a ReferenceError instead of returning undefined.

interviewQA.question: Why does typeof undeclaredVar return "undefined" while typeof x throws if let x is declared later in the block?
interviewQA.answer: Because let x IS hoisted into the block scope in the TDZ, making typeof throw ReferenceError before initialization.

lessons.title: Primitive Types, typeof Quirks & Reference Semantics
lessons.summary: JavaScript has 7 primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null) copied by value, while objects, arrays, and functions are passed by shared reference.
explanation: JavaScript has 7 primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null) copied by value, while objects, arrays, and functions are passed by shared reference.

A famous historical bug causes typeof null to return "object"—always check value === null explicitly. Use structuredClone(obj) for native deep cloning of nested data structures (including Dates, Maps, and Sets).
Check arrays with Array.isArray(x) rather than typeof x (which returns "object").

codeExample.title: Value Copy vs Reference Sharing & structuredClone

keyPoints: 7 primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol, null.
typeof null === "object" is a legacy spec quirk; use val === null.
Spread ({ ...obj }) makes a shallow copy; structuredClone(obj) makes a true deep copy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming { ...obj } deeply clones nested arrays and objects
commonMistakes.fix: Spread only clones top-level keys; nested references remain shared—use structuredClone() for deep copies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using typeof x === "object" without excluding null
commonMistakes.fix: Always guard with x !== null && typeof x === "object".

interviewQA.question: Why does typeof null return "object"?
interviewQA.answer: In JavaScript’s original 1995 implementation, values carried a 3-bit type tag where objects were 000 and null was the all-zero pointer, causing typeof to misreport null as "object".

interviewQA.question: What types cannot be cloned by structuredClone()?
interviewQA.answer: Functions, DOM nodes, and Symbol properties throw a DataCloneError when passed to structuredClone().

lessons.title: Strict Equality (===), Object.is() & Type Coercion
lessons.summary: Loose equality (==) triggers complex abstract coercion rules (like "" == 0 being true), whereas strict equality (===) compares both type and value with zero implicit conversion.
explanation: Loose equality (==) triggers complex abstract coercion rules (like "" == 0 being true), whereas strict equality (===) compares both type and value with zero implicit conversion.

Two edge cases exist even with ===: NaN === NaN is false, and +0 === -0 is true. Object.is(NaN, NaN) returns true and Object.is(+0, -0) returns false—and React uses Object.is() internally to detect state changes.
Always use === and !==; the only idiomatic exception is x == null to match both null and undefined simultaneously.

codeExample.title: Equality Edge Cases
codeExample.code:
console.log(0 === false);          // false
console.log(NaN === NaN);          // false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN));  // true
console.log(Number.isNaN('abc'));  // false (safer than global isNaN)

keyPoints: Prefer === everywhere to avoid surprising coercion bugs like [] == ![] evaluating to true.
Use Number.isNaN(x) instead of global isNaN(x), which coerces strings like "abc" to NaN.
Object.is() matches === except it treats NaN as equal to NaN and distinguishes +0 from -0.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using global isNaN("hello") expecting false
commonMistakes.fix: Global isNaN coerces its argument to a number first; use Number.isNaN() which never coerces.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking x === NaN
commonMistakes.fix: NaN is never equal to itself under ===; use Number.isNaN(x) or Object.is(x, NaN).

interviewQA.question: How does Number.isNaN() differ from global isNaN()?
interviewQA.answer: Number.isNaN() returns true ONLY if the value is already of type number and equals NaN; global isNaN() coerces non-numbers first, so isNaN("foo") returns true.

interviewQA.question: Why is null == undefined true while null == 0 is false?
interviewQA.answer: The Abstract Equality spec explicitly defines null and undefined as loosely equal only to each other and never to numbers or booleans.

lessons.title: Truthiness, Short-Circuiting & Nullish Coalescing (??)
lessons.summary: JavaScript has exactly 8 falsy values (false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN); everything else—including empty arrays [] and empty objects {}—is truthy.
explanation: JavaScript has exactly 8 falsy values (false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN); everything else—including empty arrays [] and empty objects {}—is truthy.

Using logical OR (||) for defaults breaks when valid values are 0, "", or false. Nullish coalescing (??) falls back ONLY when the left side is null or undefined, pairing cleanly with optional chaining (?.).
Use ?? for numeric, boolean, and string defaults (e.g., const port = config.port ?? 3000;).

codeExample.title: Nullish Coalescing vs Logical OR

keyPoints: Empty arrays [] and empty objects {} are TRUTHY in JavaScript.
?? triggers its right-hand fallback strictly for null and undefined (preserving 0, "", false).
Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits to undefined safely on nullish intermediate properties.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing const count = input.count || 10 when 0 is a valid count
commonMistakes.fix: Use input.count ?? 10 so 0 is preserved instead of silently replaced with 10.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing if (arr) to check whether an array is non-empty
commonMistakes.fix: [] is truthy; check arr.length > 0 explicitly.

interviewQA.question: What are all the falsy values in JavaScript?
interviewQA.answer: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, and NaN.

interviewQA.question: Why can’t you mix && or || directly with ?? without parentheses?
interviewQA.answer: The spec forbids unparenthesized mixing (e.g. a || b ?? c throws a SyntaxError) to prevent precedence bugs.

sections.title: Functions, Parameters & Scope
sections.description: Master declarations vs expressions, arrow functions, rest/spread, default parameters, and lexical scope.

lessons.title: Declarations, Expressions & Function Hoisting
lessons.summary: Function declarations are hoisted with their full body, whereas function expressions and arrow functions assigned to const follow TDZ rules.
explanation: Function declarations are hoisted with their full body, whereas function expressions and arrow functions assigned to const follow TDZ rules.

Because function declarations hoist completely, helper functions can sit cleanly below top-level orchestration logic. Function expressions are ideal for callbacks, closures, and conditional assignment.
Name your function expressions (const retry = function retry() {}) or assign clear const names so stack traces stay readable.

codeExample.title: Hoisting Difference in Practice

keyPoints: Function declarations hoist both identifier and body to the top of their enclosing scope.
Arrow functions and function expressions assigned to const/let cannot be called before initialization.
Functions are first-class values: passable as arguments and returnable from other functions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling a const arrow function before its definition line
commonMistakes.fix: Declare const arrow functions before invoking them, or use a function declaration.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring named functions inside if blocks in non-strict mode
commonMistakes.fix: Behavior varies across legacy engines; assign const/let expressions inside blocks instead.

interviewQA.question: How does hoisting differ between function foo(){} and const foo = () => {}?
interviewQA.answer: function foo(){} is fully hoisted and callable anywhere in its scope; const foo is hoisted into the TDZ and throws ReferenceError if called before its line executes.

interviewQA.question: What makes functions "first-class citizens" in JavaScript?
interviewQA.answer: They can be stored in variables, passed as callbacks, returned from higher-order functions, and assigned properties just like objects.

lessons.title: Arrow Functions vs Regular Functions
lessons.summary: Arrow functions provide concise syntax and lexically inherit this and arguments from their enclosing scope.
explanation: Arrow functions provide concise syntax and lexically inherit this and arguments from their enclosing scope.

Arrow functions cannot be invoked with new (they have no [[Construct]] internal method or prototype property) and ignore call/apply/bind for their this argument—making them ideal for array callbacks and timers, but wrong for object prototype methods that need dynamic this.
Wrap implicit object returns in parentheses: const makeUser = (name) => ({ name });—otherwise braces parse as a function body!

codeExample.title: Implicit Object Return & Lexical this

keyPoints: Arrow functions bind this lexically from where they are defined, never from how they are called.
Arrow functions have no own arguments object and cannot be used as constructors with new.
Always parenthesize implicit object literal returns: () => ({ key: val }).

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing const fn = () => { a: 1 } expecting an object return
commonMistakes.fix: JavaScript parses { a: 1 } as a labeled block returning undefined; wrap as ({ a: 1 }).

commonMistakes.mistake: Using an arrow function as an object method or DOM event listener needing this
commonMistakes.fix: Use regular method syntax { onClick() {} } when dynamic this is required.

interviewQA.question: Can you change an arrow function’s this with .bind(obj)?
interviewQA.answer: No. Arrow functions have no own this binding; call, apply, and bind ignore the first thisArg parameter.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you call new ArrowFn()?
interviewQA.answer: Throws a TypeError because arrow functions are not constructors and lack a prototype property.

lessons.title: Default Parameters, Rest & Spread Operators
lessons.summary: ES6 default parameters evaluate lazily on every call only when an argument is strictly undefined (not null or 0).
explanation: ES6 default parameters evaluate lazily on every call only when an argument is strictly undefined (not null or 0).

Rest parameters (...args) collect trailing arguments into a real Array (replacing legacy array-like arguments), while spread (...arr) expands any iterable into function calls or array/object literals.
Avoid allocating mutable default objects outside the function; ES6 default parameter expressions like (items = []) safely create a fresh array per call.

codeExample.title: Fresh Default Arrays & Rest Aggregation

keyPoints: Default parameters trigger ONLY on undefined (null passes through as null).
Rest (...args) must be the final parameter and yields a genuine Array.
Default parameter expressions are evaluated fresh on each call, avoiding shared mutable state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting default parameter (x = 5) to trigger when passing null
commonMistakes.fix: Passing null sets x to null; only undefined (or omitted arguments) activates default parameters.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing a rest parameter before another parameter (...a, b)
commonMistakes.fix: Rest must always be the last parameter or JavaScript throws a SyntaxError.

interviewQA.question: How does ...args differ from the legacy arguments object?
interviewQA.answer: ...args is a true Array supporting map/reduce/filter directly and works in arrow functions, whereas arguments is an array-like object unavailable in arrows.

interviewQA.question: What does function f(a = 1, b = a * 2) return for f(3)?
interviewQA.answer: a is 3, and b references earlier parameter a to compute 6.

lessons.title: Higher-Order Functions & Pure Function Design
lessons.summary: Higher-order functions either accept callbacks as arguments or return newly constructed functions—forming the backbone of array pipelines, debouncing, and middleware.
explanation: Higher-order functions either accept callbacks as arguments or return newly constructed functions—forming the backbone of array pipelines, debouncing, and middleware.
Pure functions always return the same output for the same inputs without mutating external state, making them trivial to unit-test, memoize, and compose.
Keep core business logic (scoring, filtering, formatting) in pure helper modules decoupled from DOM/React state.

codeExample.title: Composing a Reusable Debounce Utility

keyPoints: Higher-order functions abstract control patterns (debounce, throttle, memoize, retry).
Pure functions produce deterministic outputs and zero side effects.
Callbacks compose cleanly when data transformations return new values instead of mutating inputs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating input arrays inside helper functions passed to UI components
commonMistakes.fix: Return new arrays/objects so callers never suffer silent state aliasing bugs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating a new debounced function inside every render or event invocation
commonMistakes.fix: Instantiate debounce once outside the event handler so its timerId closure persists across calls.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between debounce and throttle?
interviewQA.answer: Debounce delays execution until calls stop for N ms (ideal for search inputs); throttle guarantees execution at most once every N ms while events fire continuously (ideal for scroll/resize).

interviewQA.question: Why are pure functions easier to test and cache?
interviewQA.answer: Because output depends exclusively on arguments with no hidden global state, enabling deterministic unit tests and safe memoization.

sections.title: Arrays, Objects & Modern Collections
sections.description: Master map/filter/reduce, ES2023 immutable array methods, destructuring, and Map/Set.

lessons.title: Declarative Array Pipelines: map, filter, reduce, flatMap
lessons.summary: Functional array methods transform collections cleanly without manual index loops.
explanation: Functional array methods transform collections cleanly without manual index loops.

map preserves length (1-to-1 transform), filter selects a subset, flatMap maps and flattens 1 level in a single pass, and reduce folds an array into any shape (sum, lookup map, grouped object). Always pass an initialValue to reduce to prevent TypeErrors on empty arrays.
Avoid calling .sort() on an array you do not own—Array.prototype.sort mutates in place and sorts lexicographically by default!

codeExample.title: Safe Reduction & Numeric Sorting

keyPoints: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparator sorts numbers as strings ("100" before "25")!
ES2023 toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced(), and with() return new arrays without mutating the original.
Always pass an explicit initial value to reduce() so empty arrays never throw.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling [10, 2, 1].sort() expecting [1, 2, 10]
commonMistakes.fix: Without a numeric comparator (a, b) => a - b, JS converts elements to strings and yields [1, 10, 2].

commonMistakes.mistake: Using .map() solely for side effects instead of .forEach() or for..of
commonMistakes.fix: Use map() only when you use its returned transformed array.

interviewQA.question: What does [10, 2, 1].sort() return and why?
interviewQA.answer: [1, 10, 2], because default sort converts values to UTF-16 strings and compares lexicographically.

interviewQA.question: How does toSorted() differ from sort()?
interviewQA.answer: sort() mutates the array in place and returns the same reference; ES2023 toSorted() returns a brand-new sorted copy leaving the original untouched.

lessons.title: Destructuring, Computed Keys & Object Utilities
lessons.summary: Destructuring unpacks nested objects and arrays concisely with renaming and fallback defaults in one expression.
explanation: Destructuring unpacks nested objects and arrays concisely with renaming and fallback defaults in one expression.
Object.entries(), Object.fromEntries(), Object.keys(), and ES2024 Object.groupBy() make object-to-array transformations ergonomic and clean.
Use Object.hasOwn(obj, key) (ES2022) instead of obj.hasOwnProperty(key), which crashes on Object.create(null) dictionaries.

codeExample.title: Destructuring, Renaming & Object.fromEntries

keyPoints: Object destructuring supports renaming ({ a: alias }) and defaults ({ b = 10 }).
Object.entries() + Object.fromEntries() lets you map/filter objects using array methods.
Object.hasOwn(obj, prop) is safer than obj.hasOwnProperty(prop).

commonMistakes.mistake: Destructuring from null or undefined without a fallback object
commonMistakes.fix: Write const { id } = payload ?? {}; to avoid TypeError: Cannot destructure property of null.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling obj.hasOwnProperty(k) on a null-prototype object
commonMistakes.fix: Use static Object.hasOwn(obj, k), which works safely on every object.

interviewQA.question: Why is Object.hasOwn(obj, key) preferred over obj.hasOwnProperty(key)?
interviewQA.answer: Objects created with Object.create(null) lack Object.prototype, and malicious objects can shadow hasOwnProperty; static Object.hasOwn() avoids both hazards.

interviewQA.question: What does Object.groupBy(items, fn) return?
interviewQA.answer: A null-prototype object grouping array items by the key returned from fn.

lessons.title: Map, Set, WeakMap & WeakSet
lessons.summary: Map and Set provide O(1) average lookup, preserve insertion order, allow any value (including objects) as keys, and avoid prototype key collisions.
explanation: Map and Set provide O(1) average lookup, preserve insertion order, allow any value (including objects) as keys, and avoid prototype key collisions.
WeakMap and WeakSet hold object keys weakly so entries are automatically garbage-collected when the key object is no longer referenced elsewhere—preventing memory leaks in caches and DOM metadata.
Use Set for O(1) membership checks and deduplication ([...new Set(arr)]) instead of repeated O(n) array.includes().

codeExample.title: O(1) Deduplication & Frequency Map

keyPoints: Map supports non-string keys, has an O(1) .size property, and avoids "__proto__" key collisions.
Set enforces uniqueness using SameValueZero (so NaN equals NaN inside a Set).
WeakMap keys must be objects (or non-registered symbols) and cannot be iterated so GC stays non-observable.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using array.includes() inside a loop over 10,000 items (O(n^2))
commonMistakes.fix: Convert the lookup list to a Set for O(1) .has() checks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to iterate or read .size on a WeakMap
commonMistakes.fix: WeakMap is intentionally non-iterable because garbage collection timing is nondeterministic.

interviewQA.question: When should you choose Map over a plain object {}?
interviewQA.answer: When keys are dynamic/untrusted user strings (preventing prototype pollution), when keys are non-strings (objects/numbers), when frequent insertions/deletions occur, or when you need .size directly.

interviewQA.question: Why can’t WeakMap store primitive string keys?
interviewQA.answer: Primitives are copied by value and not garbage-collected by object identity, so weak references cannot track their lifetime.

lessons.title: Iteration Protocols: for..of vs for..in
lessons.summary: for..of iterates VALUES of any iterable (Array, String, Map, Set, NodeList) via Symbol.iterator, whereas for..in iterates enumerable STRING KEYS including inherited prototype keys!
explanation: for..of iterates VALUES of any iterable (Array, String, Map, Set, NodeList) via Symbol.iterator, whereas for..in iterates enumerable STRING KEYS including inherited prototype keys!
Never use for..in to iterate arrays: it returns string indices ("0", "1"), skips order guarantees on custom properties, and walks up the prototype chain.
Use for..of for arrays/iterables (supports break, continue, and await cleanly), and Object.entries() with for..of for plain objects.

codeExample.title: Iterating Cleanly with for..of

keyPoints: for..of iterates values of iterables and works seamlessly with async/await and break/continue.
for..in iterates enumerable property keys including inherited prototype properties.
Array.prototype.forEach() CANNOT be exited early with break or return, and does NOT await async callbacks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using await inside arr.forEach(async (item) => ...)
commonMistakes.fix: forEach ignores returned promises and fires all iterations concurrently without waiting; use for..of or Promise.all(arr.map(...)).

commonMistakes.mistake: Using for..in on an array
commonMistakes.fix: Use for..of or standard indexed for loops for arrays.

interviewQA.question: Why doesn’t await work as expected inside array.forEach()?
interviewQA.answer: forEach executes the callback synchronously for every item and discards the returned Promise, so the enclosing async function does not wait for iterations to finish.

interviewQA.question: What makes an object iterable by for..of and spread (...)?
interviewQA.answer: Implementing a [Symbol.iterator]() method returning an iterator object with a .next() method yielding { value, done }.

sections.title: DOM Manipulation & Events
sections.description: Query elements efficiently, delegate events cleanly, prevent XSS, and observe visibility with IntersectionObserver.

lessons.title: Querying, Creating & Batching DOM Updates
lessons.summary: Modern DOM APIs (querySelector, closest, append, replaceChildren, DocumentFragment) make dynamic UI updates crisp and fast.
explanation: Modern DOM APIs (querySelector, closest, append, replaceChildren, DocumentFragment) make dynamic UI updates crisp and fast.

Avoid inserting elements inside tight loops that interleave DOM writes with layout reads (like offsetHeight), which causes forced synchronous reflow ("layout thrashing"). Batch insertions using a DocumentFragment or element.append(...nodes).
Always prefer textContent over innerHTML for dynamic user strings to eliminate XSS risks.

codeExample.title: Batching DOM Creation with DocumentFragment

keyPoints: querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList; getElementsByClassName returns a live HTMLCollection.
replaceChildren() clears and inserts new nodes cleanly in one call.
Batching reads before writes avoids forced synchronous layout thrashing.

commonMistakes.mistake:
Using innerHTML += "
  • ...
    • " inside a loop
commonMistakes.fix: Each += serializes, destroys, and re-parses the entire container DOM and drops existing event listeners; append nodes via DocumentFragment instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Interleaving style writes and offsetWidth reads inside a loop
commonMistakes.fix: Measure all elements first, then apply all style mutations together.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a live HTMLCollection and a static NodeList?
interviewQA.answer: A live HTMLCollection (getElementsByTagName) updates automatically when the DOM changes (causing infinite loops if mutating while iterating), whereas querySelectorAll returns a static snapshot NodeList.

interviewQA.question: What is layout thrashing?
interviewQA.answer: Repeatedly writing to DOM styles and immediately reading layout geometry (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) inside a loop, forcing the browser to recalculate layout synchronously on every iteration.

lessons.title: Event Propagation: Capturing, Target, Bubbling & Delegation
lessons.summary: DOM events travel in three phases: Capturing (window down to target), Target, and Bubbling (target back up to window).
explanation: DOM events travel in three phases: Capturing (window down to target), Target, and Bubbling (target back up to window).

Event Delegation attaches a SINGLE listener on a parent container and inspects event.target.closest("button[data-id]")—using constant O(1) memory even for 10,000 list rows and automatically handling newly added items.
Know the difference between event.target (the innermost clicked node, e.g., an SVG path) and event.currentTarget (the element holding the listener).

codeExample.title: Clean Event Delegation with closest()

keyPoints: event.target is the deepest clicked element; event.currentTarget is the element running the listener.
event.target.closest(selector) handles clicks on nested icons inside buttons reliably.
event.preventDefault() cancels default browser action; event.stopPropagation() stops bubbling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Checking event.target.tagName === "BUTTON" when the button contains an icon <span>
commonMistakes.fix: Clicking the icon makes event.target the <span>; use event.target.closest("button") instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing stopPropagation() with preventDefault()
commonMistakes.fix: stopPropagation stops bubbling up the DOM; preventDefault cancels native browser behavior like form submission or link navigation.

interviewQA.question: Why is Event Delegation often superior to attaching listeners to every list item?
interviewQA.answer: It uses one listener instead of N (saving memory), avoids re-attaching listeners when items are dynamically added, and simplifies cleanup.

interviewQA.question: Which common DOM events do NOT bubble?
interviewQA.answer: focus, blur, load, and scroll do not bubble (use focusin/focusout or capture phase { capture: true } instead).

lessons.title: AbortController for Clean Listener & Fetch Cleanup
lessons.summary: Passing { signal: controller.signal } to addEventListener lets you tear down dozens of listeners simultaneously with a single controller.abort() call—no need to keep references to every callback.
explanation: Passing { signal: controller.signal } to addEventListener lets you tear down dozens of listeners simultaneously with a single controller.abort() call—no need to keep references to every callback.

The exact same AbortController pattern cancels in-flight fetch() requests when a user types a new search query or navigates away, preventing race conditions where stale responses overwrite newer results.
Always attach an AbortController signal to search-as-you-type fetch calls and component-scoped window listeners.

codeExample.title: One-Line Listener & Fetch Teardown

keyPoints: AbortController removes multiple listeners cleanly via one controller.abort() call.
Aborting a fetch rejects with an AbortError—handle it separately from real network errors.
AbortSignal.timeout(5000) creates an automatic 5-second fetch timeout cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling removeEventListener with a newly created anonymous arrow function
commonMistakes.fix: Two arrow functions are distinct references so removeEventListener silently fails; use a named function or AbortController signal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring race conditions on rapid search input fetch calls
commonMistakes.fix: Abort the previous request before dispatching the next so slower old responses cannot overwrite fresh results.

interviewQA.question: Why does addEventListener({ signal }) eliminate common listener memory leaks?
interviewQA.answer: You don’t need to store matching callback references or capture flags—calling controller.abort() removes every listener registered with that signal automatically.

interviewQA.question: How do you set a 5-second timeout on fetch() in modern JS?
interviewQA.answer: Pass { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) } in the fetch options object.

lessons.title: IntersectionObserver & ResizeObserver
lessons.summary: Modern Observer APIs replace expensive scroll and resize polling listeners with asynchronous, browser-optimized callbacks.
explanation: Modern Observer APIs replace expensive scroll and resize polling listeners with asynchronous, browser-optimized callbacks.

IntersectionObserver detects when elements enter the viewport (lazy-loading media, infinite scroll, active table-of-contents highlighting), while ResizeObserver reacts to individual element box size changes cleanly.
Always call observer.disconnect() (or unobserve) when elements unmount to prevent detached DOM leaks.

codeExample.title: Lazy Visibility Detection with IntersectionObserver

keyPoints: IntersectionObserver runs off the main scroll path—no getBoundingClientRect() scroll jank.
Always call unobserve() for one-shot reveal or lazy-load triggers.
ResizeObserver observes specific element size changes, not just window resize.

commonMistakes.mistake: Polling getBoundingClientRect() on every window scroll event
commonMistakes.fix: Replace scroll geometry checks with IntersectionObserver for smooth 60fps scrolling.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting observer.disconnect() in SPA cleanup
commonMistakes.fix: Disconnect observers on component unmount so removed nodes can be garbage collected.

interviewQA.question: Why is IntersectionObserver dramatically faster than a scroll event listener?
interviewQA.answer: The browser computes intersections asynchronously off the critical scroll thread without forcing synchronous main-thread layout reflows.

interviewQA.question: What does threshold: 0.5 configure in IntersectionObserver?
interviewQA.answer: The callback fires when at least 50% of the target element’s bounding box is visible within the root viewport.

sections.title: Closures, Execution Context & this
sections.description: Master lexical environments, practical closure patterns, and the 4 rules governing this binding.

lessons.title: Lexical Scoping & Closures Under the Hood
lessons.summary: A closure is formed whenever a function retains live access to variables from its outer lexical environment even after the outer function has returned.
explanation: A closure is formed whenever a function retains live access to variables from its outer lexical environment even after the outer function has returned.

Closures capture variable BINDINGS (references), not snapshots of values—which is why incrementing a closed-over counter persists across invocations, and why var in loops shared a single binding across callbacks.
Use closures for clean data encapsulation (private state), memoization caches, and factory functions.

codeExample.title: Private State Encapsulation via Closure

keyPoints: Every function carries a hidden [[Environment]] link to its birth lexical scope.
Closures reference live bindings—mutations are visible to all functions sharing that scope.
Be mindful of retaining huge objects unintentionally inside long-lived closures.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming closures freeze the value of a variable at function creation time
commonMistakes.fix: Closures capture the live variable binding; if mutated later, the closure sees the updated value.

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating memory leaks by keeping references to huge DOM arrays inside global event closures
commonMistakes.fix: Extract only the tiny primitive ID needed before creating long-lived callbacks.

interviewQA.question: Define a closure in one clear sentence.
interviewQA.answer: A closure is the combination of a function and its lexical environment, allowing the function to read and mutate outer variables even after the outer function finishes executing.

interviewQA.question: Why did for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)) print 3, 3, 3?
interviewQA.answer: Because var is function-scoped, all three callbacks closed over the exact same i binding whose final value after the loop was 3; using let creates a separate binding per iteration.

lessons.title: The 4 Rules of this Binding
lessons.summary: For regular (non-arrow) functions, this is determined dynamically at CALL TIME using four precedence rules: new > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.method()) > default (undefined in strict mode).
explanation: For regular (non-arrow) functions, this is determined dynamically at CALL TIME using four precedence rules: new > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.method()) > default (undefined in strict mode).
Extracting a method into a standalone variable (const fn = user.greet; fn();) detaches the implicit object context, causing this to become undefined in strict mode (or window in sloppy mode).
Use ES modules or "use strict" everywhere so accidental unbound this fails loudly as undefined instead of silently corrupting globalThis.

codeExample.title: Implicit Loss vs Explicit Binding

keyPoints: Precedence: new > call/apply/bind > obj.fn() > default (undefined in strict mode).
Detaching a method (const f = obj.m) loses implicit this binding.
Arrow functions ignore all 4 rules and inherit this lexically from surrounding code.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing obj.handleClick directly to addEventListener without binding
commonMistakes.fix: Inside the DOM callback, this becomes the DOM element instead of obj; bind it or wrap in an arrow () => obj.handleClick().

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to re-bind an already-bound function with .bind() a second time
commonMistakes.fix: Once bound via .bind(), a function’s this is permanently locked (except when invoked with new).

interviewQA.question: Compare call(), apply(), and bind().
interviewQA.answer: call(thisArg, a, b) and apply(thisArg, [a, b]) invoke the function immediately with explicit this; bind(thisArg, a) returns a new permanently bound function without invoking it yet.

interviewQA.question: What does this equal inside a standalone function call in an ES module?
interviewQA.answer: undefined, because ES modules execute strictly in strict mode by default.

lessons.title: Memoization & Partial Application with Closures
lessons.summary: Closures power practical performance and composition utilities like function memoization and currying.
explanation: Closures power practical performance and composition utilities like function memoization and currying.

A memoize wrapper stores previous input-to-output results in a private Map so repeated expensive pure computations return in O(1) time. Pair with a bounded cache size in production so long-running processes never exhaust RAM.
Only memoize pure functions; caching functions that depend on Date.now() or mutable external state causes stale bugs.

codeExample.title: Bounded Memoization Factory

keyPoints: Memoization trades O(n) memory to collapse exponential repeated subproblems to linear/O(1).
Use a Map inside the closure so cache storage stays completely encapsulated.
Avoid unbounded memo caches on arbitrary user inputs (use LRU eviction if needed).

commonMistakes.mistake: Memoizing with JSON.stringify(args) on objects containing circular references or functions
commonMistakes.fix: Use primitive keys or nested WeakMaps for object-key memoization.

commonMistakes.mistake: Memoizing an impure function that reads changing server or DOM state
commonMistakes.fix: Memoize only deterministic pure functions.

interviewQA.question: What is currying vs partial application?
interviewQA.answer: Currying transforms f(a, b, c) into nested unary calls f(a)(b)(c); partial application fixes some arguments upfront to produce a function taking the remaining arguments.

interviewQA.question: Why can unbounded memoization cause memory leaks in Node.js servers?
interviewQA.answer: If unique keys keep arriving forever (like user IDs or timestamps), the closure Map grows indefinitely until the V8 heap runs out of memory.

lessons.title: Prototypes, Prototype Chain & Class Syntax
lessons.summary: JavaScript classes are clean syntactic sugar over prototypal delegation: every instance links via [[Prototype]] to its constructor’s .prototype object.
explanation: JavaScript classes are clean syntactic sugar over prototypal delegation: every instance links via [[Prototype]] to its constructor’s .prototype object.

When you read obj.toString(), the engine walks obj -> obj’s [[Prototype]] -> Object.prototype -> null. Methods defined inside a class live once on ClassName.prototype (shared across all instances), whereas class fields like onClick = () => {} allocate a fresh copy on every instance.
Use private class fields (#balance) for true runtime encapsulation enforced by the JavaScript engine.

codeExample.title: ES2022 Private Class Fields & Prototype Methods

keyPoints: class methods live on ClassName.prototype (shared); arrow class fields live per-instance.
Private fields (#field) cannot be accessed or inspected outside the class body.
Object.getPrototypeOf(x) is the standard replacement for legacy __proto__.

commonMistakes.mistake: Defining arrow methods on classes instantiated 100,000 times
commonMistakes.fix: Arrow class fields allocate a new function object per instance; prefer prototype methods for high-volume data classes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating built-in Object.prototype or Array.prototype directly
commonMistakes.fix: Monkey-patching global prototypes breaks third-party libraries and future ECMAScript methods.

interviewQA.question: Where are regular methods vs arrow class fields stored in memory?
interviewQA.answer: Regular class methods live once on Class.prototype and are shared via delegation; arrow class fields are created separately on each instance during construction.

interviewQA.question: What happens if external code tries to read acct.#balance?
interviewQA.answer: JavaScript throws a SyntaxError because # private fields are strictly enforced at parse and runtime.

sections.title: Asynchronous JS: Promises & Async/Await
sections.description: Master Promise states, error propagation, async/await concurrency patterns, and Fetch API pitfalls.

lessons.title: Promise States, Chaining & Rejection Handling
lessons.summary: A Promise represents an eventual completion or failure and transitions irreversibly from pending to either fulfilled or rejected.
explanation: A Promise represents an eventual completion or failure and transitions irreversibly from pending to either fulfilled or rejected.
Every .then() and .catch() returns a NEW Promise—returning a plain value resolves the next link, returning a Promise adopts its state, and throwing rejects down the chain until a .catch() handles it.
Always return promises inside .then() chains and terminate chains with .catch() (or try/catch in async functions) to avoid unhandled rejections.

codeExample.title: Clean Promise Chain with Error Recovery
codeExample.code:
Promise.resolve(10)
  .then((n) => n * 2)
  .then((n) => { if (n > 15) throw new Error('Too high'); return n; })
  .catch((err) => 0)
  .then((final) => console.log('Recovered:', final));

keyPoints: A Promise settles at most once; subsequent resolve/reject calls are silently ignored.
Returning a value from .catch() recovers the chain into a fulfilled state.
finally() runs on both fulfillment and rejection without altering the resolved value (unless it throws).

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to return a nested Promise inside .then()
commonMistakes.fix: Without return, the outer chain resolves immediately to undefined before the inner request finishes.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrapping an already Promise-returning function in new Promise(...) ("Promise constructor antipattern")
commonMistakes.fix: Return the existing Promise directly instead of adding redundant wrappers that swallow errors.

interviewQA.question: What are the three possible states of a Promise?
interviewQA.answer: pending, fulfilled, and rejected (fulfilled and rejected are collectively called "settled").

interviewQA.question: What does .finally(() => 999) pass to the next .then()?
interviewQA.answer: The original resolved value—finally ignores its own return value unless it throws or returns a rejected Promise.

lessons.title: async/await & Avoiding Sequential Waterfalls
lessons.summary: async functions always return a Promise, and await suspends only the current async function (not the browser main thread) until the awaited Promise settles.
explanation: async functions always return a Promise, and await suspends only the current async function (not the browser main thread) until the awaited Promise settles.
A common performance bug is awaiting two independent requests sequentially—doubling latency! Kick off independent promises together with Promise.all() so they run concurrently.
Wrap await calls in try/catch/finally for crisp error handling and loading-state teardown.

codeExample.title: Parallel Concurrency vs Sequential Waterfall

keyPoints: An async function ALWAYS wraps its return value in a Promise.
Use Promise.all() for independent async work instead of back-to-back awaits.
await pauses only the enclosing async function; other UI events keep running smoothly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Awaiting independent API calls sequentially (await fetchA(); await fetchB();)
commonMistakes.fix: Launch them in parallel with Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]).

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing return await fn() outside a try/catch vs inside try/catch
commonMistakes.fix: Inside try/catch you MUST write return await fn() so rejections are caught locally; without await, the rejection bypasses catch!

interviewQA.question: Why is return await promise() required inside a try/catch block?
interviewQA.answer: Without await, the function returns the pending Promise directly and exits the try block before the rejection happens, bypassing the catch block completely.

interviewQA.question: What does async function f() { return 5; } return?
interviewQA.answer: A Promise fulfilled with 5.

lessons.title: Promise Combinators: all, allSettled, race & any
lessons.summary: JavaScript offers four static Promise combinators tailored to distinct concurrency and resilience requirements.
explanation: JavaScript offers four static Promise combinators tailored to distinct concurrency and resilience requirements.

Promise.all fails fast on the first rejection; Promise.allSettled waits for every promise and returns { status, value | reason } for each; Promise.race settles on the very first settled promise (win or fail); Promise.any resolves on the first FULFILLMENT and rejects with AggregateError only if ALL fail.
Use Promise.allSettled when loading independent dashboard widgets so one flaky endpoint never blanks the whole page.

codeExample.title: Resilient Widget Fetching with Promise.allSettled

keyPoints: Promise.all: all succeed, or fail-fast on first rejection.
Promise.allSettled: never rejects; reports full outcome array for every promise.
Promise.race: first settled (resolved OR rejected); Promise.any: first fulfilled.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using Promise.all when partial failures are acceptable
commonMistakes.fix: Use Promise.allSettled to render successful panels while showing localized error states for failed ones.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing Promise.race with Promise.any when racing mirrors
commonMistakes.fix: Use Promise.any for fastest healthy mirror (ignores fast 500 errors); use Promise.race for timeouts.

interviewQA.question: How do Promise.race() and Promise.any() differ if the fastest promise rejects?
interviewQA.answer: Promise.race immediately rejects with that error; Promise.any ignores the rejection and keeps waiting for another promise to fulfill (throwing AggregateError only if every promise rejects).

interviewQA.question: What does Promise.all([]) return?
interviewQA.answer: A Promise that immediately fulfills with an empty array [].

lessons.title: Fetch API Gotchas & Custom Error Classes
lessons.summary: Unlike Axios, fetch() ONLY rejects on network failures or aborted requests—an HTTP 404 or 500 response still RESOLVES with response.ok === false!
explanation: Unlike Axios, fetch() ONLY rejects on network failures or aborted requests—an HTTP 404 or 500 response still RESOLVES with response.ok === false!

Always check if (!res.ok) throw new HttpError(res.status, ...) before calling res.json(). Extending Error with custom subclasses and using the ES2022 { cause } option preserves full debugging context.
Create a small reusable fetchJson() wrapper that enforces response.ok, timeouts, and typed error classes.

codeExample.title: Safe fetchJson Helper with HTTP Status Guard

keyPoints: fetch() resolves on HTTP 404 and 500; always verify response.ok before parsing JSON.
A Response body stream can only be consumed once (call res.clone() if needed twice).
Use new Error("Context", { cause: originalErr }) to chain root causes cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming .catch() triggers on an HTTP 500 response from fetch()
commonMistakes.fix: Check if (!response.ok) explicitly and throw a structured error.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling response.json() twice on the same Response object
commonMistakes.fix: Response bodies are single-use ReadableStreams; store the parsed value in a variable.

interviewQA.question: When does fetch() actually reject its returned Promise?
interviewQA.answer: Only on network errors (DNS failure, offline, CORS block) or request cancellation via AbortController—never on HTTP 4xx/5xx status codes.

interviewQA.question: What is the ES2022 Error { cause } option used for?
interviewQA.answer: Wrapping low-level errors in higher-level domain errors while preserving the original error object and stack trace on err.cause.

sections.title: Prototypes, Classes & Object Internals
sections.description: Understand prototype chains, ES6 classes, private fields, property descriptors, and structured cloning.

lessons.title: Prototype Chains, Object.create & Property Lookup
lessons.summary: JavaScript uses prototypal delegation rather than classical class copying: every object holds an internal [[Prototype]] link walked upward whenever a property is not found directly on the object.
explanation: JavaScript uses prototypal delegation rather than classical class copying: every object holds an internal [[Prototype]] link walked upward whenever a property is not found directly on the object.

Methods defined on Constructor.prototype are shared by every instance in O(1) memory instead of being duplicated per object. Object.create(null) creates a truly empty dictionary object with no inherited Object.prototype keys.
Prefer Object.hasOwn(obj, key) (ES2022) over obj.hasOwnProperty(key) so dictionary objects created with Object.create(null) never crash.

codeExample.title: Inspecting the Prototype Chain & Safe Own Checks

keyPoints: Property lookups traverse obj -> [[Prototype]] -> ... -> Object.prototype -> null.
Object.hasOwn(obj, key) safely checks own properties even on null-prototype objects.
Writing to obj.prop always creates/updates an OWN property without mutating the prototype.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating Object.prototype or Array.prototype directly
commonMistakes.fix: Extending built-in prototypes causes naming collisions with future ECMAScript standards and third-party libraries.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling obj.hasOwnProperty("k") on an untrusted or Object.create(null) object
commonMistakes.fix: Use Object.hasOwn(obj, "k") to avoid TypeError or prototype-shadowing exploits.

interviewQA.question: What happens when you assign instance.sharedProp = 42 if sharedProp exists on the prototype?
interviewQA.answer: JavaScript creates a new own property sharedProp = 42 on instance (shadowing the prototype property) rather than mutating the prototype—unless the prototype defines a setter.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between __proto__ and Function.prototype?
interviewQA.answer: Function.prototype is the object assigned as the [[Prototype]] of instances created with new Fn(); __proto__ is a legacy accessor for reading/setting an object’s [[Prototype]] (use Object.getPrototypeOf instead).

lessons.title: ES6 Classes, Private #Fields & Static Members
lessons.summary: ES6 classes provide clean, strict-mode syntactic sugar over prototype inheritance while adding true runtime-enforced private fields (#balance), static methods, and extends/super semantics.
explanation: ES6 classes provide clean, strict-mode syntactic sugar over prototype inheritance while adding true runtime-enforced private fields (#balance), static methods, and extends/super semantics.
Unlike TypeScript private (which disappears at runtime), JavaScript #private fields are genuinely inaccessible outside the class body—even via Object.keys() or Reflect.ownKeys().
Use private #fields to guard internal invariants and always call super() before touching this inside a subclass constructor.

codeExample.title: True Encapsulation with #Private Fields

keyPoints: Class bodies automatically execute in strict mode and are NOT hoisted for use before declaration (TDZ).
Private #fields enforce true runtime encapsulation—accessing acc.#balance outside throws a SyntaxError.
Subclass constructors must invoke super() before referencing this.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accessing this before super() in a derived class constructor
commonMistakes.fix: Derived classes allocate this inside super(); reading this earlier throws ReferenceError.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing a class method directly as a callback (btn.onclick = acc.deposit) losing this
commonMistakes.fix: Bind methods or wrap in an arrow function (() => acc.deposit(10)) so this stays bound.

interviewQA.question: Are JavaScript class declarations hoisted like function declarations?
interviewQA.answer: Class declarations are bound in scope but remain in the Temporal Dead Zone until evaluated—instantiating before the class line throws ReferenceError.

interviewQA.question: How do JavaScript #private fields differ from _underscore conventions?
interviewQA.answer: _balance is still a public enumerable property; #balance is engine-enforced private storage completely hidden from outside access and JSON.stringify.

lessons.title: Property Descriptors, Object.freeze & Shallow vs Deep Cloning
lessons.summary: Every JavaScript object property carries hidden descriptor flags: value, writable, enumerable, and configurable (or get/set accessors).
explanation: Every JavaScript object property carries hidden descriptor flags: value, writable, enumerable, and configurable (or get/set accessors).

Object.freeze(obj) makes own properties non-writable and non-configurable, but it is SHALLOW—nested objects remain mutable! For true deep clones of data structures (including Date, Map, Set, and circular refs), use native structuredClone().
Use structuredClone(state) instead of JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(state)) so Dates, Sets, Maps, and undefined values are not corrupted.

codeExample.title: Deep Cloning with structuredClone vs Shallow Freeze

keyPoints: Object.freeze() is shallow: nested objects/arrays inside a frozen object can still be mutated.
structuredClone() deep-copies Dates, Maps, Sets, RegExps, ArrayBuffers, and circular references natively.
JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) silently drops undefined, functions, Symbols, and converts Dates to strings.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Object.freeze({ user: { role: "guest" } }) prevents obj.user.role = "admin"
commonMistakes.fix: Object.freeze only freezes top-level properties; recursively freeze nested objects if deep immutability is needed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing functions or DOM nodes to structuredClone()
commonMistakes.fix: structuredClone throws DataCloneError on functions and DOM nodes—clone plain data models only.

interviewQA.question: Why is structuredClone() usually better than JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))?
interviewQA.answer: structuredClone preserves Date, Map, Set, RegExp, typed arrays, and circular references without crashing or silently corrupting types.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between Object.seal() and Object.freeze()?
interviewQA.answer: Object.seal prevents adding or deleting properties (configurable: false) while still allowing existing writable values to change; Object.freeze also sets writable: false.

lessons.title: Error Hierarchies, Custom Errors & Defensive Validation
lessons.summary: Structured error handling separates programmer bugs from recoverable runtime failures using custom Error subclasses with machine-readable error codes and ES2022 { cause } chaining.
explanation: Structured error handling separates programmer bugs from recoverable runtime failures using custom Error subclasses with machine-readable error codes and ES2022 { cause } chaining.
Because JavaScript lets anyone throw non-Error values (like strings), always normalize caught values in catch (err) blocks using err instanceof Error before reading err.message or err.stack.
Design domain error classes (ValidationError, AuthError, NetworkError) so callers can branch cleanly with instanceof.

codeExample.title: Custom Error Subclass with Cause Chaining

keyPoints: Always extend the built-in Error class so stack traces and instanceof Error work properly.
Set this.name = this.constructor.name for readable logs and telemetry.
Use { cause } to wrap low-level errors without losing original root-cause diagnostics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing catch (e) {} empty catch blocks that swallow errors silently
commonMistakes.fix: At minimum log, rethrow, or surface a clear recovery state so failures never vanish invisibly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Throwing raw strings (throw "failed") instead of Error objects
commonMistakes.fix: Strings lack stack traces and break instanceof Error checks across error boundaries.

interviewQA.question: Why should you throw new Error("...") instead of throw "..."?
interviewQA.answer: Error instances capture stack traces, support structured properties like .cause, and work consistently with instanceof checks and debugging tools.

interviewQA.question: When does a finally block execute relative to a return inside try?
interviewQA.answer: finally ALWAYS executes before the function returns to its caller—even if try or catch executes a return or throw statement.

sections.title: Browser Storage, Fetch & Modern Web APIs
sections.description: Persist client data reliably with Storage & IndexedDB, observe intersections cleanly, and build resilient HTTP clients.

lessons.title: localStorage, sessionStorage & Cross-Tab Synchronization
lessons.summary: Web Storage provides synchronous key-value string persistence (~5MB per origin): localStorage survives browser restarts while sessionStorage clears when the tab closes.
explanation: Web Storage provides synchronous key-value string persistence (~5MB per origin): localStorage survives browser restarts while sessionStorage clears when the tab closes.

Because localStorage throws QuotaExceededError when full or SecurityError in restricted iframes/private modes, always wrap reads/writes in try/catch and listen to the window "storage" event to sync state across open tabs.
Design storage behind an async-ready adapter interface so migrating from localStorage to IndexedDB or Supabase later requires zero UI rewrites.

codeExample.title: Safe JSON Storage Wrapper with Cross-Tab Sync

keyPoints: Web Storage stores strings only—serialize objects with JSON.stringify and validate on parse.
The window "storage" event fires in OTHER open tabs on the same origin when localStorage changes.
Never store sensitive credentials or unencrypted tokens in localStorage (XSS readable).

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming localStorage.getItem() never throws or returns corrupted JSON
commonMistakes.fix: Always guard both storage access and JSON.parse inside try/catch with a clean fallback.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting the "storage" event to fire in the SAME tab that called setItem()
commonMistakes.fix: The native storage event only notifies OTHER tabs/windows on the same origin.

interviewQA.question: What is the key security risk of storing JWT access tokens in localStorage?
interviewQA.answer: Any JavaScript running on the page (including XSS payloads or compromised third-party scripts) can read localStorage directly, whereas HttpOnly cookies are invisible to JS.

interviewQA.question: How does sessionStorage differ from localStorage?
interviewQA.answer: sessionStorage is scoped per browser tab/session and cleared when the tab closes; localStorage persists across restarts and is shared across all tabs of the origin.

lessons.title: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver & MutationObserver
lessons.summary: Modern Observer APIs replace expensive scroll and resize polling loops with asynchronous, browser-scheduled callbacks that never force synchronous layout thrashing.
explanation: Modern Observer APIs replace expensive scroll and resize polling loops with asynchronous, browser-scheduled callbacks that never force synchronous layout thrashing.
IntersectionObserver powers lazy loading, infinite scroll, and active table-of-contents highlighting; ResizeObserver tracks individual container dimensions cleanly for responsive charts and canvases.
Always call observer.disconnect() when cleaning up components or routes so observed DOM nodes can be garbage collected.

codeExample.title: Lazy-Tracking Active Lesson Section with IntersectionObserver

keyPoints: IntersectionObserver detects viewport visibility off the hot scroll path with zero layout thrash.
ResizeObserver fires when a specific element’s box size changes—even without a window resize.
Always unobserve() or disconnect() observers on teardown to prevent memory leaks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Polling element.getBoundingClientRect() inside a window scroll listener
commonMistakes.fix: Reading layout geometry on every scroll frame triggers forced reflows; use IntersectionObserver instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to disconnect observers in single-page app route changes
commonMistakes.fix: Active observers hold references to DOM subtrees; always call observer.disconnect() on unmount.

interviewQA.question: Why is IntersectionObserver faster than checking getBoundingClientRect() in a scroll event?
interviewQA.answer: IntersectionObserver batches visibility calculations inside the browser’s rendering pipeline asynchronously without forcing synchronous main-thread layout reflows.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between window "resize" events and ResizeObserver?
interviewQA.answer: window resize only fires when the viewport changes; ResizeObserver fires whenever a specific element resizes (e.g., when a sidebar collapses or font size changes).

lessons.title: URL, URLSearchParams & History Navigation APIs
lessons.summary: The built-in URL and URLSearchParams classes parse, validate, and serialize URLs and query strings safely—eliminating brittle string concatenation and regex bugs.
explanation: The built-in URL and URLSearchParams classes parse, validate, and serialize URLs and query strings safely—eliminating brittle string concatenation and regex bugs.
URLSearchParams automatically percent-encodes special characters (spaces, &, =, Unicode) and supports multi-value parameters via .getAll() and .append().
Use new URL(path, window.location.origin) to construct safe links and keep search/filter state reflected cleanly in query parameters.

codeExample.title: Safe Query Parameter Building with URL & URLSearchParams

keyPoints: URLSearchParams handles percent-encoding automatically so & and + never break query strings.
new URL(input) validates syntax and throws TypeError on malformed URLs.
Check url.protocol against an allowlist (https:, http:) before navigating user-supplied links.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concatenating query strings manually like `?q=${input}` without encodeURIComponent
commonMistakes.fix: A search for "C# & .NET" breaks parameter parsing; URLSearchParams encodes everything cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating window.location.search directly when you only want to update filters in an SPA
commonMistakes.fix: Use history.replaceState or router searchParams so the page does not trigger a full reload.

interviewQA.question: Why does `?q=C#` break if not encoded properly?
interviewQA.answer: The # character starts a URL fragment identifier on the client, truncating the query parameter before it ever reaches the server; URLSearchParams encodes it as %23.

interviewQA.question: How does history.pushState differ from history.replaceState?
interviewQA.answer: pushState adds a new entry to the browser Back stack, whereas replaceState updates the current entry without adding a Back step (ideal for live search filters).

lessons.title: Intl APIs: Dates, Numbers, Currencies & Relative Time
lessons.summary: The built-in ECMAScript Internationalization API (Intl) formats numbers, currencies, dates, plurals, and relative times ("3 days ago") accurately across hundreds of locales with zero bundle bloat.
explanation: The built-in ECMAScript Internationalization API (Intl) formats numbers, currencies, dates, plurals, and relative times ("3 days ago") accurately across hundreds of locales with zero bundle bloat.
Intl.DateTimeFormat, Intl.NumberFormat, and Intl.RelativeTimeFormat respect regional calendars, separators, and plural rules automatically—replacing bulky third-party formatting libraries.
Reuse Intl formatter instances (new Intl.NumberFormat(...)) outside hot loops for dramatically faster formatting.

codeExample.title: Zero-Dependency Formatting with Intl

keyPoints: Intl APIs ship natively in every browser and Node.js with zero KB added to your JS bundle.
Intl.RelativeTimeFormat("en", { numeric: "auto" }) outputs natural phrases like "yesterday".
Cache Intl.*Format instances instead of recreating them inside every table row render.

commonMistakes.mistake: Formatting currency with "$" + price.toFixed(2) for international users
commonMistakes.fix: Currency symbols, decimals, and separators vary globally; use Intl.NumberFormat with style: "currency".

commonMistakes.mistake: Creating new Intl.DateTimeFormat() inside a 5,000-row map loop
commonMistakes.fix: Instantiate the formatter once outside the loop and call formatter.format(date) repeatedly.

interviewQA.question: What advantage does Intl.Collator have over simple string comparison (a < b) when sorting names?
interviewQA.answer: Intl.Collator sorts accurately according to locale-specific alphabet rules, accents, case folding, and optional numeric order ("Lesson 2" before "Lesson 10").

interviewQA.question: How do you format "Lesson 2" before "Lesson 10" using native JavaScript?
interviewQA.answer: Use new Intl.Collator(undefined, { numeric: true }).compare(a, b).

sections.title: The Event Loop & Concurrency Internals
sections.description: Trace the Call Stack, Web APIs, Microtask Queue, Macrotask Queue, and requestAnimationFrame accurately.

lessons.title: Call Stack, Microtasks & Macrotasks Execution Order
lessons.summary: JavaScript executes synchronously on a single Call Stack, then drains the ENTIRE Microtask Queue (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before pulling the next single Macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, UI events).
explanation: JavaScript executes synchronously on a single Call Stack, then drains the ENTIRE Microtask Queue (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before pulling the next single Macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, UI events).

Because every microtask queued during microtask draining ALSO runs before the next macrotask or browser paint, an infinite recursive Promise loop freezes the page completely, whereas recursive setTimeout yields to the browser between ticks.
Always trace interview Event Loop puzzles in 3 passes: 1) Synchronous top-level code (including new Promise executor!), 2) All queued Microtasks, 3) Macrotasks.

codeExample.title: Classic Interview Event Loop Trace

keyPoints: The executor function passed to new Promise((resolve) => { ... }) runs SYNCHRONOUSLY!
Microtasks (Promise.then, await continuations, queueMicrotask) always run before macrotasks (setTimeout).
Browser rendering/paint happens between macrotasks after microtasks drain.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming code inside new Promise((resolve) => console.log("A")) runs asynchronously
commonMistakes.fix: The Promise constructor callback executes immediately and synchronously; only .then/.catch/.finally callbacks are queued as microtasks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Spawning unbounded recursive microtasks to defer heavy work
commonMistakes.fix: Use setTimeout or scheduler.yield() to break up long tasks so browser paints are not starved.

interviewQA.question: Why can a runaway queueMicrotask loop freeze UI rendering while setTimeout(..., 0) does not?
interviewQA.answer: The Event Loop drains the microtask queue completely before rendering a frame; macrotasks like setTimeout allow paint cycles between turns.

interviewQA.question: How does await x desugar in terms of the Microtask Queue?
interviewQA.answer: Everything before await runs synchronously, and the code after await is scheduled as a microtask continuation once x resolves.

lessons.title: requestAnimationFrame, Idle Callbacks & Yielding Long Tasks
lessons.summary: A smooth 60fps frame gives the main thread just 16.6ms for JS, style, layout, and paint; tasks exceeding 50ms degrade Interaction to Next Paint (INP).
explanation: A smooth 60fps frame gives the main thread just 16.6ms for JS, style, layout, and paint; tasks exceeding 50ms degrade Interaction to Next Paint (INP).

Schedule visual DOM animation steps inside requestAnimationFrame (synced right before paint), defer non-urgent analytics to requestIdleCallback, and chunk heavy loops by yielding back to the event loop.
Keep event handlers lean so button clicks produce immediate visual feedback well under 100ms.

codeExample.title: Chunking Heavy Work Without Blocking Input

keyPoints: Long synchronous tasks (>50ms) block user clicks and hurt INP.
requestAnimationFrame synchronizes updates cleanly to display refresh rate.
Yielding via setTimeout(0) or scheduler.yield() lets the browser handle pending input and paints.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running a 400ms synchronous filter/sort inside an input keydown handler
commonMistakes.fix: Debounce input or offload heavy CPU work to a Web Worker.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using setInterval(fn, 16) for visual animations instead of requestAnimationFrame
commonMistakes.fix: setInterval drifts out of sync with monitor VSync and wastes battery in background tabs; rAF auto-pauses in hidden tabs.

interviewQA.question: Why does requestAnimationFrame save battery compared to setInterval?
interviewQA.answer: Browsers automatically pause rAF callbacks in background tabs and align execution directly to the display’s VSync refresh rate.

interviewQA.question: What Core Web Vital measures UI responsiveness to clicks and key presses?
interviewQA.answer: Interaction to Next Paint (INP), targeting <= 200ms.

lessons.title: Web Workers & Off-Main-Thread Architecture
lessons.summary: Web Workers run JavaScript in genuine OS background threads with isolated heaps, keeping the UI thread 100% responsive during heavy parsing, search indexing, or cryptography.
explanation: Web Workers run JavaScript in genuine OS background threads with isolated heaps, keeping the UI thread 100% responsive during heavy parsing, search indexing, or cryptography.
Workers have NO access to the DOM or window; they communicate via structured-cloned messages (postMessage) or zero-copy Transferable objects (like ArrayBuffer) that hand off ownership in O(1) time.
Use Transferable ArrayBuffers when passing megabytes of binary/image data to a Worker to avoid expensive copy overhead.

codeExample.title: Zero-Copy ArrayBuffer Transfer to a Worker

keyPoints: Web Workers execute on a real background thread with zero DOM access.
postMessage uses structured clone by default; pass Transferables ([buffer]) for zero-copy handoff.
Terminate unneeded workers with worker.terminate() to free OS thread resources.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trying to update document.getElementById inside a Web Worker
commonMistakes.fix: Compute results in the Worker and postMessage lightweight results back to the main thread to render.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a transferred ArrayBuffer on the main thread after postMessage(buf, [buf])
commonMistakes.fix: Once transferred, the sender’s buffer byteLength becomes 0 (detached).

interviewQA.question: What happens to an ArrayBuffer on the sender side after transferring it via postMessage(data, [buffer])?
interviewQA.answer: Ownership moves in O(1) time and the original buffer becomes detached (byteLength 0), preventing unsafe concurrent memory access.

interviewQA.question: Can Web Workers call fetch() and access IndexedDB?
interviewQA.answer: Yes—Workers support fetch, WebSockets, IndexedDB, crypto, and timers, just not DOM or synchronous localStorage.

lessons.title: ES Modules: Live Bindings, Tree-Shaking & Dynamic import()
lessons.summary: ES Modules (import/export) are statically analyzable, execute in strict mode once per module URL, and export LIVE read-only bindings rather than static value copies.
explanation: ES Modules (import/export) are statically analyzable, execute in strict mode once per module URL, and export LIVE read-only bindings rather than static value copies.

Because static imports are parsed before execution, bundlers like Vite/Rollup can tree-shake unused exports cleanly. Dynamic import("./heavy.js") loads chunks lazily on demand (just like course JSON files on IT Courses!).
Avoid side effects at module top level so bundlers can safely tree-shake unused exports.

codeExample.title: Dynamic Code-Splitting with import()

keyPoints: ES Module exports are live bindings: mutations inside the exporting module reflect in importers.
Modules are singletons—evaluated once and cached by URL across all importers.
Static imports enable dead-code elimination (tree-shaking); dynamic import() enables route/feature code splitting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Attempting to reassign an imported binding directly (count = 5)
commonMistakes.fix: Imported bindings are read-only views; mutate via an exported setter function instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Barrel index.js files importing heavy side-effectful modules eagerly
commonMistakes.fix: Keep exports pure and mark "sideEffects": false in package.json for optimal tree-shaking.

interviewQA.question: How do ES Module exports differ from CommonJS module.exports?
interviewQA.answer: ES Modules are statically analyzed (enabling tree-shaking), asynchronous, and expose live read-only bindings; CommonJS require() is synchronous, dynamic, and copies primitive exports by value.

interviewQA.question: What does dynamic import(path) return?
interviewQA.answer: A Promise that resolves to the Module Namespace Object containing all named exports and default export.

sections.title: Metaprogramming, Generators & Memory
sections.description: Master Symbols, Iterators, Generators, Proxy/Reflect reactivity, and V8 memory leak prevention.

lessons.title: Symbols & Custom Iterable Protocols
lessons.summary: Symbols create guaranteed-unique property keys that never collide with string keys and stay invisible to Object.keys() and JSON.stringify().
explanation: Symbols create guaranteed-unique property keys that never collide with string keys and stay invisible to Object.keys() and JSON.stringify().
Well-known symbols like Symbol.iterator, Symbol.asyncIterator, and Symbol.toPrimitive let custom classes integrate seamlessly with for..of, spread (...), and string coercion.
Implement [Symbol.iterator]() on custom collections (like pagination cursors or ranges) so consumers can use native for..of loops.

codeExample.title: Custom Iterable Range with Symbol.iterator

keyPoints: Every Symbol("id") call produces a globally unique token (Symbol("x") !== Symbol("x")).
Symbol.for("key") uses the global symbol registry so cross-realm code can share a symbol.
Implementing [Symbol.iterator] unlocks for..of, array destructuring, and spread syntax.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting Symbol properties to appear in JSON.stringify(obj)
commonMistakes.fix: JSON.stringify ignores Symbol-keyed properties completely.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Symbol("tag") === Symbol("tag")
commonMistakes.fix: Each Symbol() is unique; use Symbol.for("tag") only when shared lookup is intentional.

interviewQA.question: How do you inspect Symbol keys on an object if Object.keys() skips them?
interviewQA.answer: Use Object.getOwnPropertySymbols(obj) or Reflect.ownKeys(obj) (which returns both string and symbol own keys).

interviewQA.question: What does Symbol.iterator enable?
interviewQA.answer: Any object implementing [Symbol.iterator]() becomes natively consumable by for..of, spread (...), destructuring, Array.from(), and Set/Map constructors.

lessons.title: Generators (function*) & Async Generators
lessons.summary: Generator functions (function*) pause execution at each yield expression and resume lazily on demand via .next(), enabling infinite sequences and pull-based streams with O(1) memory.
explanation: Generator functions (function*) pause execution at each yield expression and resume lazily on demand via .next(), enabling infinite sequences and pull-based streams with O(1) memory.
Async generators (async function*) combine yield with await, letting you stream paginated API pages effortlessly using for await (const page of fetchPages()).
Prefer generators for lazy pipelines over giant datasets so you never allocate millions of intermediate array elements.

codeExample.title: Lazy Infinite ID Generator & Paginated Stream

keyPoints: Calling a generator function returns a suspended Generator object—body code doesn’t run until first .next().
yield pauses execution and returns { value, done: false } cleanly.
async function* pairs with for await...of to consume paginated APIs or Node streams lazily.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling gen() expecting the body up to the first yield to run immediately
commonMistakes.fix: A generator starts suspended; you must call .next() (or iterate with for..of) to begin execution.

commonMistakes.mistake: Spreading an infinite generator ([...idGenerator()])
commonMistakes.fix: Spreading pulls values until done: true, which hangs forever on an infinite generator; take a bounded slice instead.

interviewQA.question: What is a real-world production use case for async generators?
interviewQA.answer: Streaming cursor-paginated database or REST API results lazily—fetching the next page only when the consumer requests more items.

interviewQA.question: What does yield* otherIterable do inside a generator?
interviewQA.answer: It delegates iteration directly to another generator or iterable, yielding each of its values cleanly.

lessons.title: Proxy & Reflect Metaprogramming
lessons.summary: A Proxy wraps a target object and intercepts fundamental operations (property reads, writes, deletes, function calls) via handler traps—powering reactive frameworks like Vue 3 and Immer.
explanation: A Proxy wraps a target object and intercepts fundamental operations (property reads, writes, deletes, function calls) via handler traps—powering reactive frameworks like Vue 3 and Immer.
Always forward default behavior inside Proxy traps using Reflect (Reflect.get, Reflect.set) rather than raw target[prop], so receiver/getter this-binding and boolean return contracts work accurately.
Remember that Proxy traps require returning true from the set trap in strict mode, otherwise JavaScript throws a TypeError.

codeExample.title: Reactive Validation Proxy with Reflect

keyPoints: Proxy intercepts get, set, has, deleteProperty, apply, construct, and more.
Pair every Proxy trap with the matching Reflect method to preserve receiver semantics.
Returning false from a set trap in strict mode throws a TypeError.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to return true (or Reflect.set(...)) in a Proxy set trap
commonMistakes.fix: Strict mode throws TypeError: "set" on proxy returned falsish.

commonMistakes.mistake: Accessing target[prop] directly instead of Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver) on objects with getters
commonMistakes.fix: Raw target[prop] binds getter this to target instead of the Proxy, bypassing reactive tracking.

interviewQA.question: Why is Reflect.get(target, prop, receiver) preferred over target[prop] inside a Proxy get trap?
interviewQA.answer: When target has an inherited getter that reads another property via this.x, passing receiver ensures this stays the Proxy so nested reads are also intercepted.

interviewQA.question: Can a Proxy intercept private #classFields directly?
interviewQA.answer: Private fields are stored in internal slots on the target; calling methods via a Proxy requires binding method this or avoiding raw #field access on the Proxy receiver.

lessons.title: Garbage Collection, Memory Leaks & Debugging Tools
lessons.summary: V8 uses generational mark-and-sweep garbage collection, reclaiming objects no longer reachable from GC roots (global scope, active call stack, live DOM listeners).
explanation: V8 uses generational mark-and-sweep garbage collection, reclaiming objects no longer reachable from GC roots (global scope, active call stack, live DOM listeners).

The top four JavaScript memory leaks are: (1) forgotten timers/setIntervals, (2) unremoved window/document event listeners, (3) detached DOM trees retained in JS arrays or closures, and (4) unbounded in-memory caches.
Use Chrome DevTools Heap Snapshot comparison (Take Snapshot -> perform action -> Take Snapshot -> filter Detached) to verify zero retained leaks.

codeExample.title: Leak-Free Cache with WeakRef / Cleanup Pattern

keyPoints: Modern JS GC uses reachability (mark-and-sweep), NOT simple reference counting—so unreachable circular references ARE collected cleanly.
Always pair setInterval, WebSockets, Observers, and window listeners with deterministic teardown.
WeakMap/WeakSet prevent cache entries from keeping removed objects alive.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming circular references (a.b = b; b.a = a) always leak in modern JS
commonMistakes.fix: Mark-and-sweep collects unreachable cycles automatically; leaks happen when something stays reachable from a live root.

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing removed DOM elements inside a module-level array
commonMistakes.fix: Detached DOM subtrees keep every sibling and parent reference in memory until cleared.

interviewQA.question: How does mark-and-sweep garbage collection handle circular references?
